Maladaptive Strategies.value: go along with whatever others want to feel safe
Being alone in a room or building
Crowded places such as shopping centres or public events

Threat.value: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
The people responsible have faced no consequences
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.item: Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, nocturnal checking for one's own immediate physical safety is not impossible, but paired with the rest of the profile it introduces a more direct personal-danger threat theme that is not otherwise represented in triggers or memory. The triggers and memory items are centered on reminders of the loved one's trauma/loss rather than the patient's own current physical danger, so this specific item is the least coherent threat item.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
issues.explanation: Self-blame based on one's character can occur after a loved one's trauma, but here it sits awkwardly beside appraisals focused on institutional failure and lack of accountability, which externalize blame to others. This is not impossible, but this item is the most internally tensioned within the appraisal node and less clearly linked to the rest of the profile than guilt on recall would be.

vignette:
Tariq Mansouri is a 52-year-old widowed Lebanese-American actor who presents with a PCL-5 score of 66, seeking psychological support approximately fourteen months after witnessing the violent assault of his teenage son outside a crowded concert venue in their home city. The incident occurred on a warm Friday evening when Tariq and his son, Dani, had stepped away from the main crowd to find a quieter exit. A confrontation escalated rapidly between a group of young men nearby, and before Tariq could move, Dani was struck and knocked to the ground, sustaining serious injuries while the crowd surged indifferently around them. Tariq recalls standing frozen for what he estimates were several seconds - seconds he has since replayed with an almost forensic, unbearable precision - before he dropped to his knees beside his son. The sounds that surrounded that moment were particular and relentless: the roar of the dispersing crowd, the distant bass thrum of the music still playing inside, and above everything else, the crying of a young child somewhere in the chaos, a sound that seemed to Tariq both incongruous and indelible.

Dani survived and has since recovered physically, but Tariq has not recovered from what he saw. His memories of the event do not arrive as a coherent narrative. They come instead in disconnected photographs - Dani's shoe at an odd angle on the concrete, a stranger's face looking down without stopping, his own hands, which he remembers studying as though they belonged to someone else. When these images surface, they bring with them a wave of guilt so acute that Tariq has described it as physically nauseating. He had been standing right there. He has come to believe, with a certainty that no reassurance has shifted, that a different man - a faster man, a braver man - would have intervened in time.

This conviction has shaped the months that followed in ways that have quietly dismantled large portions of his life. Tariq is a working actor with a modest but consistent career in regional theatre and television, and his professional environment has become one of the primary sites of his distress. Rehearsals frequently involve recorded sound effects, ambient crowd noise, and on two occasions this past year, scenes involving children in distress. Each time, the sound of a child crying - whether on a monitor in a production booth or from a fellow actor's performance - has produced in Tariq an immediate and overwhelming response: a flooding of strong fear and shame that he cannot contain or explain to his colleagues. He has begun going along with whatever directors and castmates ask of him without pushback, agreeing to blocking, scheduling, and scene choices he finds distressing, because disagreement feels dangerous in a way he cannot fully articulate. He had come to understand compliance as a form of protection, as though keeping others contented around him might prevent another catastrophic loss of control.

Outside of work, Tariq has stopped attending public events entirely. The shopping centre near his apartment, which he once visited routinely, has become impassable to him - the density of bodies, the ambient noise, the unpredictability of crowds all converge into something that feels to him not like discomfort but like genuine threat. He is equally unable to be alone. He will leave lights on in every room, call his sister on the phone for hours, or sit in the hallway outside his apartment rather than remain inside by himself. Yet even with others present and even when told directly that he is safe, Tariq finds the reassurance impossible to absorb. Safety, as a felt reality, has simply ceased to be available to him.

What has deepened his distress beyond the symptoms themselves is his understanding of what happened after the assault. The individuals responsible were never charged. The venue's security response was, in his view, catastrophically inadequate. He carries a specific and unresolved fury at the institutions he had trusted implicitly - the venue, the responding officers, the legal process - and what frightens him most is that his rage has nowhere legitimate to go.

Tariq sought help only after missing a significant professional commitment, a stage production he had rehearsed for three months, because he could not bring himself to enter the building on opening night. He arrives hoping, tentatively, that he might be able to work again without dread. He is most afraid that the guilt he carries will prove to be the correct verdict on who he is.
